results.title: GPU Cloud Pricing Explained: On-Demand, Reserved, Bare Metal
highlights:
# GPU Cloud Pricing Explained: On-Demand, Reserved, and Bare Metal

GPU cloud pricing is more than an hourly rate. This guide explains on-demand, reserved, and bare metal options, when each makes financial sense, and how utilization affects costs. Compare GMI Cloud GPU rates, break-even points, and hidden expenses to choose the right pricing model.

October 21, 2026

GPU cloud pricing looks simple on a rate card, but the hourly number hides two separate decisions: How you commit to paying for capacity, and how much of the server you actually get. Understanding both is what separates a GPU bill that tracks useful work from one that pays for idle hardware.

- On-demand buys flexibility: You pay per GPU-hour with no commitment and can stop at any time, which suits experiments, bursty jobs, and workloads whose utilization you have not measured yet.
- Reserved pricing buys a lower rate: Committing to a term lowers the effective hourly price, but you pay for every hour of the term, so it only saves money when utilization stays above the break-even point set by the discount.
- Bare metal is a deployment model, not a billing term: It gives you the whole physical server with root access and no hypervisor, which can be bought on demand or reserved, and NVIDIA has measured virtualized training running 12% slower than bare metal.
- Published rates are only a starting point: On GMI Cloud, on-demand rates start at $2.60 per GPU-hour for H100, $3.20 for H200, $5.00 for B200, and $8.00 for GB200 as of October 2026, while committed plans are discounted and storage and networking are priced separately.
- Utilization decides which model wins: Cast AI’s 2026 analysis of production clusters found average enterprise GPU utilization of roughly 5%, which shows how easily reserved capacity turns into paid idle time. Matching the pricing model to measured usage is the single biggest lever on GPU cost.

...

On GMI Cloud, all GPU resources are dedicated, single-tenant instances priced per GPU-hour, with the rate depending on GPU type and deployment model. Pay-as-you-go containers have no expiration date and can be terminated at any time, and pay-as-you-go managed clusters are charged by the minute with no upfront cost, as GMI explains in its guide to comparing container, bare metal, and managed cluster quotes.

...

### On-Demand GPU Rates on GMI Cloud

The table below shows GMI Cloud’s published starting rates, taken from the GMI Cloud pricing page in October 2026. Rates vary by region and deployment model and can change with promotions, so treat them as starting points and confirm the live rate in the GMI Cloud console before you budget.

| GPU | On-demand rate (October 2026) | Availability (October 2026) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA H100 | From $2.60 per GPU-hour | Available now |
| NVIDIA H200 | From $3.20 per GPU-hour | Available now |
| NVIDIA B200 | From $5.00 per GPU-hour | Limited availability |
| NVIDIA GB200 | From $8.00 per GPU-hour | Available now |
| NVIDIA GB300 | Pre-order | Pre-order |

...

On GMI Cloud, containers can run on prepaid plans with renewal periods from one day to three years, and a prepaid container cannot be terminated before its rental period ends. Committed usage plans are discounted relative to on-demand, with volume and custom pricing handled by the sales team. Before you confirm an order, the console shows the list price, the discount, and the estimated monthly total, which makes it easy to compare a committed plan with the on-demand equivalent.

### Short-Term Reservations Are Now Common

Reservations no longer have to mean multi-year contracts. Many providers now sell short reservations sized for a single training run. AWS, for example, lets customers reserve GPU capacity through EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML with a start date up to eight weeks ahead and durations from one day up to 182 days. GMI Cloud’s prepaid terms starting at one day follow the same logic: Reserve exactly the window you need, then release it.

...

The GPU-hour rate usually covers compute only. On GMI Cloud, storage and networking are priced separately when you allocate them, and several of these line items can outweigh a small difference in GPU rates. Persistent storage is one, since container-local data does not survive reconfiguration and workloads that need durable data need a volume. Public IP addresses are another. GMI Cloud bills Elastic IPs by the minute on pay as you go, and they keep billing after they are disassociated until you release them, even when the container they served has been terminated.

...

A practical sequence works for most teams. Start on demand and measure real GPU utilization for a few weeks. Commit only the baseline you are sure to use, and keep peaks on demand. Move long-running, network-heavy training to bare metal once the workload is stable. Revisit the mix every quarter, because both your usage and the market rates will change.

results.title: Cluster Capacity Planning for AI Teams: How Much Compute
highlights:
November 05, 2026

...

- Training compute follows a simple formula: Total training FLOPs are about 6 × parameters × tokens, which predicts the 3.8 × 10²⁵ FLOPs Meta reported for Llama 3 405B on 15.6 trillion tokens to within about 1%.
- Efficiency turns FLOPs into GPU-hours: At 40% model FLOPs utilization on H100s rated at 989 dense BF16 TFLOPS, pretraining an 8B model on 1 trillion tokens needs about 33,700 GPU-hours, or about 5.5 days on 256 GPUs.
- Inference is sized by memory first, then throughput: Llama 3 70B needs about 0.33 MB of BF16 KV cache per token, so 32 concurrent requests at 8,192 tokens add roughly 86 GB on top of 140 GB of weights.
- Most clusters are oversized, not undersized: Cast AI measured average GPU utilization of 5% across roughly 23,000 Kubernetes clusters in 2026, while optimized environments reach about 50%. A plan sized to measured demand avoids paying for capacity that never runs.
- Price the plan at today’s rates: On GMI Cloud, H100 capacity starts at $2.60 and H200 at $3.20 per GPU-hour (as of October 2026), which puts the 8B pretraining example at about $87,600 before reliability overhead. Capacity planning is how a team spends that budget on results instead of idle GPUs.

...

For inference, serverless inference scales to zero with no idle cost and covers the uncertain layer of demand, while dedicated endpoints and reserved GPUs cover the base. As of October 2026, the pricing page lists H100 from $2.60 per GPU-hour, H200 from $3.20, B200 from $5.00 with limited availability, and GB200 from $8.00, with commitment-based pricing for reserved capacity quoted per customer. See the GPU page for hardware details.

results.title: Serverless GPU Inference vs Dedicated Endpoints | GMI Cloud
highlights:
The right choice depends on how steady your traffic is, how strict your latency targets are, and how much control you need over the model.

October 13, 2026

Serverless inference and dedicated endpoints run the same models on the same GPUs, but they bill, scale, and behave very differently under load. The right choice depends on how steady your traffic is, how strict your latency targets are, and how much control you need over the model.

...

### Per-Token Versus Per-GPU-Hour Pricing

Serverless pricing tracks usage exactly. If your application processes no tokens overnight, the bill for those hours is zero. Per-token rates also carry time-limited promotions in the console. In October 2026, for example, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash was listed at 40% off, at $0.18 per million input tokens instead of $0.30. Dedicated pricing tracks time. On GMI Cloud, a dedicated endpoint created from the console runs on one H200 GPU with 10 CPUs and 100 GB of memory at $4.50 per hour per replica (GMI Cloud console, as of October 2026), so a single replica running around the clock for a 730-hour month costs about $3,285. Raw GPU compute without the managed inference layer is listed separately, from $2.60 per GPU-hour for an H100 and $3.20 for an H200 on the GMI Cloud pricing page. Check the GMI Cloud pricing page for current rates before modeling your own numbers. Rates can change with promotions, and GMI Cloud also offers commitment-based pricing for reserved capacity, so confirm the figure that applies to you in the GMI Cloud console before you budget.

results.title: Hyperscaler vs Specialized GPU Cloud: Total Cost Compared
highlights:
November 05, 2026

On a total cost basis, a specialized GPU cloud usually costs less than a hyperscaler for GPU-heavy training and inference, because the GPU-hour gap is around 2× and the extra line items mostly add to the hyperscaler side. Hyperscalers still win when your data, managed services, or committed spend already live there, so the answer depends on what the rest of the bill looks like.

- The GPU-hour gap is about 2×: AWS lists H200 Capacity Blocks (p5e) at $6.866 per GPU-hour and H100 (p5) at $5.970, while GMI Cloud lists H200 from $3.20 and H100 from $2.60 per GPU-hour (all as of October 2026).
- The GPU line is not the whole bill: AWS charges $0.09 per GB for the first 10 TB of monthly internet egress after a 100 GB free allowance, and its Business Support+ plan adds 9% of the first $10,000 of monthly charges and 7% of the next $70,000.
- Identical GPUs do not deliver identical throughput: NVIDIA routinely sees 8 to 12% training gaps between cloud deployments and its reference architecture on the same hardware, including a GB200 NVL72 case that ran 12 to 14% slower in a virtual machine than on bare metal.
- A worked month makes the gap concrete: One 8× H200 node with 20 TB of egress and Business Support+ comes to about $44,964 on AWS Capacity Block pricing, against an $18,688 GPU line on GMI Cloud plus whatever storage and networking the quote adds (October 2026 prices).
- Hyperscalers still win some cases: When terabytes of training data, a managed data stack, or a large committed-spend agreement already sit with one hyperscaler, moving GPUs elsewhere can add egress and engineering costs that erase the rate gap. The comparison only works when every line is on the table.

GPU prices stopped falling in 2026. Cast AI’s 2026 State of Kubernetes Optimization Report, as reported by SDxCentral, noted that AWS raised H200 Capacity Block prices by 15% in January 2026, and AWS’s own Capacity Blocks pricing page now says reservation rates are updated with supply and demand, with the next update scheduled for January 2027. When the biggest line on an AI budget moves like that, the choice of where to run GPUs deserves a real total cost comparison rather than a glance at two hourly rates.

...

### Specialized GPU Cloud Rates

Specialized GPU clouds usually price per GPU-hour directly. As of October 2026, the GMI Cloud pricing page lists H100 from $2.60 per GPU-hour, H200 from $3.20, B200 from $5.00 with limited availability, and GB200 from $8.00. The page describes the resources as dedicated NVIDIA GPUs with no shared environments, available on demand or reserved, with lower unit costs through commitment-based pricing. Committed rates are quoted per customer.

| GPU | AWS EC2 Capacity Block (per GPU-hour) | GMI Cloud on demand (from, per GPU-hour) | AWS ÷ GMI |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 | $5.970 (p5) | $2.60 | About 2.3× |
| H200 | $6.866 (p5e) / $7.895 (p5en) | $3.20 | About 2.1× to 2.5× |
| B200 | $14.208 (p6-b200) | $5.00 (limited availability) | About 2.8× |
| Basis | AWS pricing page, US regions, as of October 2026 | GMI pricing page, as of October 2026 | List rates, before discounts |

...

Both models discount for commitment, but in different ways. AWS Capacity Blocks are prepaid for a fixed window at the rate in force when you buy, and the rate itself moves with supply and demand. Savings Plans and reserved terms lower on-demand prices in exchange for a one- or three-year commitment. GMI Cloud’s pricing page describes commitment-based savings for reserved capacity and sustained deployments, with the option to start on demand and move to committed terms as workloads stabilize. Whichever you choose, compare committed offers at the same term and GPU count.

...

As of October 2026, the pricing page lists H100 from $2.60 per GPU-hour, H200 from $3.20, B200 from $5.00 with limited availability, and GB200 from $8.00, with reserved capacity and commitment-based pricing available on request. GMI’s GPU page notes that Trend Micro uses GMI Cloud GPU clusters as a more cost-effective foundation for AI workloads it previously ran on Oracle Cloud, and that Mirelo AI reports 40% lower training costs and 20% faster training. When you request a quote, ask for storage, networking, egress, and support terms in writing so the comparison table above can be completed line by line.

results.title: Which Charges Continue After a GPU Job Stops on Containers, Bare Metal, and Managed Clusters?
results.author: Colin Mo
highlights:
Which Charges Continue After a GPU Job Stops on Containers, Bare Metal, and Managed Clusters?

# Which Charges Can Continue After Your GPU Job Stops on Container, Bare-Metal, and Managed-Cluster Services?

November 02, 2026

A job finishing, a machine stopping, and a resource being deleted are three separate events, and the charges around a GPU run attach to resources rather than to the job. When a training script exits, the container, server, or cluster it ran on is not removed along with it, while attached resources such as a public IP, and any prepaid term, follow their own end dates. On GMI Cloud's GPU infrastructure, each deployment form has a defined end-of-life action: a pay-as-you-go container is terminated, a bare-metal server or a managed cluster (in early access) is deleted from its list, and an Elastic IP is released on its own. Cost control after a run is therefore a short, ordered teardown of whatever the next run will not use.

Container and bare-metal rows in the console open their orders through View Order, which shows the order number, billing method, status, and amount, and the Orders page under Billing and Usage keeps the full history. Teardown and reconciliation happen in the same place, which makes it practical to compare container, bare-metal, and managed-cluster costs on one account after the work is done, not only on the quote.

...

### Containers: the plan decides when billing can end

A pay-as-you-go container runs without an end date, and its More actions menu terminates it whenever you choose. A job's exit does not terminate it, and the container stays on the account under its pay-as-you-go order until it is terminated. When nothing else is planned for that container, terminating it soon after the job exits closes the gap.

A prepaid container runs for its rental period, and terminating it early is not part of a prepaid plan. Its cost is fixed when the plan is bought, so the decision that matters comes at renewal. Renew Plan offers extensions from one day to three years and shows the new end time and price before payment; extend only when the next run is scheduled, and to the shortest period that covers it.

...

Ending a job does not by itself remove a managed cluster's worker nodes, which belong to the cluster rather than to the job. A pay-as-you-go cluster is charged by the minute with no upfront cost, so a cluster with no work planned for the weekend is one to delete on Friday. A prepaid cluster is billed for its term. The cluster list shows each cluster's billing method next to its node count and status.

...

Renew when the next run is on the calendar, and pick the shortest extension that covers it. Renewal can be done at any time while the container is running, and the Renew page shows the new end time and price before payment. Renewing before the current end time keeps the container running without interruption.

results.title: GB300 NVL72 Pilot to Full Rack: Acceptance Criteria and Capacity Commitments
results.author: Colin Mo
highlights:
November 01, 2026

A pilot can only pass if "pass" was written down as numbers before the first job ran, and the same document should say what passing triggers: how many full racks are held for you, for how long, at what configuration and price, and what either side may do if the pilot fails or a date moves. Agree four things before the pilot starts: measurable acceptance criteria, a capacity hold you can exercise by notice, a validity period for the configuration and the price, and exit terms. GMI Cloud takes GB300 NVL72 on pre-order through our sales team, and commitment options are agreed in that same conversation, so a buyer can table all four terms alongside the reservation request. More broadly, GMI pricing lets workloads move from on-demand to dedicated or committed deployments as they stabilize, without being pushed into a long-term commitment too early.

...

> Example clause: "Provider will hold two (2) GB300 NVL72 racks for Customer from the pilot start date until thirty (30) days after the Acceptance Date (the Hold Period). The Acceptance Date is the day both parties sign the pilot acceptance report, whether it records a pass or a fail, or, if no report is signed, fifteen (15) days after the scheduled pilot end date. A provider-side retest, or a pilot extension agreed for an inconclusive result, extends the Hold Period by its length. Customer may reserve the held racks by written notice during the Hold Period, on the term, rate, and configuration set out in Schedule B. If Customer gives no notice, the hold ends without charge."

...

Price needs the same treatment. Schedule B should state the committed rate together with the term it assumes and keep both valid until the hold period ends, because the rate depends on that term: GMI pricing prices on-demand and committed usage differently. The fabric and storage lines that come with the racks need their own rates and the same validity date in that schedule. Leave them out, and a held rack can arrive with a compute rate that held and a storage line that moved.

A worked timeline makes the dates concrete. Assume a four-week pilot that starts in week 1. The acceptance report is signed in week 5, the 30-day hold runs to roughly week 9, and the reservation signed inside that window carries its own delivery window and acceptance test for the racks. If the report stalls, the clause's fallback date starts the 30 days anyway.

results.title: Comparing Managed B200, B300, and NVL72 Quotes With Different Delivery and Commitment Terms
results.author: Colin Mo
highlights:
Comparing Managed B200, B300, and NVL72 Quotes With Different Delivery and Commitment Terms

# How Should You Compare Managed B200, B300, and NVL72 Quotes When Delivery Dates, Minimum Commitments, and Capacity Guarantees Differ?

November 01, 2026

Two quotes at the same hourly rate produce different totals once billing starts at different events, one at contract signature and the other when your team can run jobs. Compare managed Blackwell quotes on one project timeline instead of on rate: place each delivery window against your need-by date, count the GPU-hours each minimum commitment obliges you to pay for, price the interim capacity a late delivery would force you to buy, and record what each provider actually guarantees. On GMI Cloud today, the Blackwell lineup (B200, B300, GB200 NVL72, GB300 NVL72) is taken as pre-orders while H100 and H200 can be run immediately, and our pricing covers both on-demand use and committed structures, so our sales team can price a Blackwell pre-order and the H100 or H200 capacity that would run before it side by side.

For teams that need Blackwell capacity on a firm project date, that pairing is what makes a provider worth shortlisting: a committed rate for the rack or nodes you plan around, plus capacity you can run on before they arrive. A lower rate tied to a later date or a larger minimum often costs more over the project.

## Read delivery status as a date range

For each quote, record five things next to the rate:

- Status. Available now or pre-order.
- Delivery unit. An NVL72 rack is a single 72-GPU NVLink domain, while HGX B200 and B300 systems come eight GPUs to a node. Ask whether a late rack can be handed over in part or only as a whole, and whether node orders can arrive in tranches.
- Earliest and latest handover date. Use the latest date in every calculation.
- Slack. Your need-by date minus the latest handover date and the validation time you plan after handover. Negative slack is a number of weeks you'll have to cover with other capacity.
- Quote validity. The date the rate and terms expire. A pre-order quote that expires before the provider can confirm allocation needs its validity extended in writing.

...

Minimum commitments come in a few forms: a GPU count held for a term (take-or-pay), a total spend over the term, or a ramp in which the committed count rises on set dates. For a fixed GPU count:

Committed GPU-hours = committed GPUs _ hours in the term

A ramp is summed stage by stage, each stage's GPU count multiplied by its hours. A total-spend commitment converts to GPU-hours only at a fixed system and rate, so a spend pool shared across B200, B300, and NVL72 is tracked in spend rather than in hours. Then compute what each used hour really costs:

Effective rate = committed spend ÷ GPU-hours your workload actually uses

Committing to 72 GPUs (one NVL72 rack) when the job needs 64 raises the effective rate by 72 ÷ 64, or 12.5%, so a 10% lower list rate becomes a slightly higher effective one. A ramp schedule that tracks your real growth curve does the reverse: it keeps committed hours close to used hours, so the effective rate stays near the committed rate.

## Price delay and substitute hardware before they happen

A delivery slip has two costs: the interim GPU-hours you buy on hardware available now, and whatever a later launch costs your business. Keep the second as its own line rather than folding it into the GPU math.

Size interim capacity against the same acceptance metric, not the same GPU count. If the interim hardware needs more GPUs to hit your step time or p95 latency, the interim GPU-hours rise in proportion. Ask, too, whether interim spend can be credited toward the Blackwell commitment.

...

A quote with no term and a short notice period can be stopped soon after you give notice. A twelve-month take-or-pay commitment may leave the remaining months due if the project is cancelled halfway through, and that figure belongs next to the rate when the project itself is uncertain.

...

## Bring your need-by date to sales

Contact our sales team with your need-by date, the GPU count your workload is shaped for, and the longest term you can commit to. Ask for the Blackwell pre-order and any interim H100 or H200 capacity to be quoted together, so both sit on the timeline you use for every other bid.

results.title: Comparing Container, Bare-Metal, and Managed-Cluster GPU Proposals When Support Differs
results.author: Colin Mo
highlights:
November 01, 2026

Put every proposal on one responsibility table that lists each operational task the workload needs, from GPU driver updates to recovering a failed node, and marks who owns that task under each proposal. A proposal with more included support moves rows from your column into the provider's, so the comparison becomes fair only after your team's rows are priced in engineer hours and added to the infrastructure line. GMI Cloud can scope all three forms against the same brief on its GPU infrastructure. All three proposals come from one console on GMI's Cluster Engine: Container Service, Bare Metal GPU, and Managed GPU Cluster (in early access), each on dedicated single-tenant GPUs priced per GPU-hour.

GPU prices on GMI Cloud vary by SKU, GPU type, and region, so the brief fixes one GPU type, one region, and one billing term before anyone writes a proposal. With those matched, the proposals differ in node specification and included support.

results.title: What to Include in an RFQ for Like-for-Like Managed B200, B300, and NVL72 Quotes
results.author: Colin Mo
highlights:
November 01, 2026

The first field in a Blackwell RFQ should describe the workload and the metric that proves the capacity works, before any GPU model appears: the model, its precision, the job type, and a number such as step time or p95 latency that every bidder has to size against. After that come hardware counts in stated units, network and storage in stated units, managed scope and support, and a response sheet every bidder fills in the same way. A provider is worth shortlisting for like-for-like quotes when it can answer each of those fields as a separate line. On GMI Cloud GPU infrastructure, every GPU is dedicated and single-tenant and priced per GPU-hour, a unit the rest of the form can be converted into.

At GMI, the Blackwell rows of such an RFQ cover B200 worker nodes for managed clusters, B300 as a hardware option for Prime Inference, and GB200 NVL72 and GB300 NVL72 racks, all in pre-order today, while H100 and H200 are available now.

...

- Status takes one of four values: included, separate line, not offered, or not quoted. A blank cell counts as not quoted, never as zero.
- Any difference from the requested value goes in the deviation column with its reason, not in a cover letter.
- An alternative system gets its own sheet, so a B200 alternate never overwrites the B300 row it replaces.
- Every sheet carries a validity date for the configuration and for the pricing tab.
